title: Mootness and voluntary cessation
summary: A case that began with standing may continue after a defendant stops the challenged conduct unless the defendant meets the demanding standard for voluntary-cessation mootness.
notes:
Mootness asks whether an actual controversy remains after filing. Standing asks whether the plaintiff could properly invoke the court’s authority when the suit began. Laidlaw distinguishes the two because a defendant could otherwise stop a challenged practice while litigation proceeds and remain free to resume it after dismissal.

Under the assigned voluntary-cessation discussion, a defendant asserting mootness bears the heavy burden of making it absolutely clear that the alleged wrongdoing cannot reasonably be expected to recur. The Court rejected the Fourth Circuit’s treatment of Laidlaw’s substantial compliance and closure as automatically eliminating the case. Its standing analysis relied on violations ongoing when the complaint was filed and on the deterrent effect of civil penalties.

The casebook also identifies the capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review exception. The supplied printed 1229 fragment discusses an agency’s continuing defense of generation-shifting authority, but the preceding page is outside the supplied assignment. That fragment supports a limited illustration that a government’s continuing assertion of disputed authority can bear on recurrence; it does not provide the entire West Virginia mootness analysis.
